questions.q: What is autotrophic nutrition?
questions.a: Making one's own food from simple substances (CO2 and water) using sunlight and chlorophyll, as green plants do.

questions.q: Why are plants called autotrophs?
questions.a: They prepare their own food by photosynthesis and do not depend on other organisms for food.

questions.q: Name the raw materials a plant uses to make food.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide from air, water and minerals from soil, plus sunlight and chlorophyll.

questions.q: What is heterotrophic nutrition?
questions.a: Taking ready-made food from other organisms, as animals and fungi do.

questions.q: Name three types of heterotrophic nutrition in plants.
questions.a: Parasitic (cuscuta), insectivorous (pitcher plant) and saprotrophic (fungi on bread).

questions.q: Give one example of a plant that is a heterotroph.
questions.a: Cuscuta (amarbel), a parasite that sucks food from host plants.

questions.q: Write the word equation of photosynthesis.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide + water + sunlight (with chlorophyll) -> carbohydrate (glucose) + oxygen.

questions.q: Why are leaves called the food factories of plants?
questions.a: Their cells hold chlorophyll, which captures sunlight to make food by photosynthesis.

questions.q: How do plants get carbon dioxide for photosynthesis?
questions.a: Through tiny pores called stomata on the leaf surface, which open to take in air.

questions.q: What are stomata?
questions.a: Tiny pores on the leaf surface through which gases and water vapour pass.

questions.q: Which cells control the opening and closing of stomata?
questions.a: Guard cells - they swell to open the pore and shrink to close it.

questions.q: Why do stomata need to open only sometimes?
questions.a: Opening loses water vapour, so plants open stomata for CO2 while limiting water loss.

questions.q: Name the main parts of a cell.
questions.a: Cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and (in plants) a cell wall and vacuole.

questions.q: What is the function of chloroplasts?
questions.a: They hold chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

questions.q: Why is the nucleus called the control centre of the cell?
questions.a: It stores DNA and directs all the cell's activities.

questions.q: What are parasitic plants?
questions.a: Plants that take ready food from another living plant (the host) using special sucking roots.

questions.q: Name a parasitic plant and its host type.
questions.a: Cuscuta (amarbel) grows on trees and hedges, drawing food from them.

questions.q: How does the host suffer from a parasite?
questions.a: It loses nutrients and water, grows weakly and may die.

questions.q: Why do pitcher plants trap insects although they are green?
questions.a: They grow in nitrogen-poor soil, so insect protein supplies the nitrogen they cannot get from soil.

questions.q: How does a pitcher plant catch its prey?
questions.a: The leaf forms a pitcher with sweet juice; insects slip in and are digested by juices inside.

questions.q: Name another insectivorous plant.
questions.a: Venus flytrap (also sundew, bladderwort).

questions.q: What is saprotrophic nutrition?
questions.a: Feeding on dead and decaying matter by secreting juices and absorbing them - as fungi do.

questions.q: Give two examples of saprotrophs.
questions.a: Bread mould (Rhizopus) and mushrooms growing on damp rotting material.

questions.q: How do fungi digest their food outside the body?
questions.a: They release digestive juices onto the food, breaking it down, then absorb the nutrients.

questions.q: What is symbiosis?
questions.a: A partnership where two organisms live together and both benefit.

questions.q: Describe the symbiosis in lichen.
questions.a: An alga makes food by photosynthesis and a fungus holds water and shelter - both live as one body.

questions.q: How do rhizobium bacteria and pulses help each other?
questions.a: Rhizobium lives in root nodules of gram and peas, turning air nitrogen usable, while the plant feeds it.

questions.q: How is soil fertility restored after a cereal crop?
questions.a: Farmers grow legume crops or add nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which refill soil nitrogen.

questions.q: Why are leguminous crops used in rotation?
questions.a: Rhizobium in their root nodules enriches soil with nitrogen for the next crop.

questions.q: Name the bacterium that fixes nitrogen in pulse roots.
questions.a: Rhizobium, living symbiotically in the root nodules of gram, peas and beans.
